The fuel itself had to be trucked forward, and the trucks burned fuel doing it—a ratio that worsened with every kilometer the front advanced. Ammunition, too, was consumed on a scale no peacetime exercise had prepared us for; the Russians did not break when the first shells fell, and so we fired again, and again. I remember a supply officer at a forward dump near Orsha, a reservist with grey at his temples, showing me his ledgers with a kind of grim humor. "The armies ask for what they need," he said, "and I send them what I can. The difference between those two numbers is the war."

And the land, that third assumption—that we could live off it—proved the cruelest illusion of all. The Soviets withdrew before us, and where they could not carry their stores, they burned them. What the retreating Red Army left, the scorched earth orders had already spoiled: grain fields fired, wells fouled, livestock driven off or slaughtered. The peasant population, when we met it, had little enough for itself. I saw a village where our foragers found nothing but a sack of potatoes buried under a floorboard, and the men who found it were ashamed to take it. An army of three million cannot eat the countryside it has just emptied.

By August the reports from the panzer groups had acquired a litany I would come to know by heart: fuel short, ammunition short, tires worn to the carcass, horses—for the infantry divisions still marched on hooves and feet—dying in the traces. The great envelopments at Smolensk were won, but they were won by units that had outrun their supply and then had to sit and wait, sometimes for a week, for the columns to catch them. In that waiting the Russians rebuilt their defenses, and the timetable that had promised Moscow before the autumn rains slipped away from us.

We did not lose the war in the mud of October, though that is where men like to place it. We began losing it in June and July, in the widening gap between what the front demanded and what the railheads could deliver—a gap that no amount of courage at the sharp end could close.

title: popular science book|what black holes reveal about space and time
text:
Black holes are where the universe keeps its most radical secrets about space and time. For most of history, space and time seemed like the plain stage on which everything else happened: a fixed backdrop, a universal clock ticking away for everyone at the same rate. Black holes demolish that comfortable picture. They are not just strange objects sitting in space; they are places where the nature of space and time themselves becomes visible, almost embarrassingly so.

Start with the most basic fact about a black hole: its event horizon. This is not a surface in any ordinary sense. There is no wall there, no membrane you could touch. It is a boundary defined entirely by causality, a one-way frontier where the geometry of spacetime tilts so steeply that every possible path into the future leads inward. Nothing about the horizon is locally dramatic; an astronaut crossing it would notice nothing special at the moment of passage. And yet it marks the point of no return, not because of some force pushing back, but because the future itself has been redirected. In this sense a black hole is a machine for revealing that the future is not a universal river. It is a direction in spacetime, and spacetime can be bent.

That bending is the heart of the matter. Einstein's general relativity describes gravity not as a pull between masses but as the curvature of spacetime caused by energy and momentum. A black hole is the most extreme curvature we know of, and it makes the abstraction concrete. Clocks run slower deeper in a gravitational field. Near a black hole this is not a subtle effect. A clock hovering close to the horizon ticks measurably slower than one far away, and as it approaches the horizon the slowdown becomes extreme. Fall toward a black hole and, from the perspective of distant observers, your time stretches out; you appear to freeze and fade at the horizon, your signals redshifted into silence. From your own perspective, though, your watch keeps ticking normally. Both descriptions are correct. Time is not absolute; it is personal, and gravity shapes it.

The horizon also scrambles our intuitions about space. Inside it, the radial direction behaves in a way we normally associate with time: it points inexorably toward the singularity, and you cannot turn around any more than you can turn around in time outside. Space and time swap roles, or at least our labels for them lose their usual meanings. This is not poetry; it falls directly out of the mathematics of curved spacetime.

Then there is the information problem, which sharpens the question of what black holes do to the past. Quantum mechanics says that the complete state of a system today determines its future and can, in principle, be run backward to reconstruct its past. But a black hole that forms and later evaporates via Hawking radiation seems to erase what fell in, leaving only thermal radiation with no memory of the details. If that radiation truly carries no information, quantum mechanics is incomplete. If it does carry information, as most physicists now believe, then the radiation must encode the black hole's interior in some deeply scrambled form. Either way, black holes force us to confront whether the past is recoverable and what it means for information to be preserved in a universe with gravity.

Finally, black holes reveal that space and time are not passive. They can be heated, they can radiate, they can store entropy proportional to area rather than volume, hinting that spacetime itself has a microscopic structure we do not yet understand. In the end, black holes are less interesting as objects than as windows. They show us that space and time are flexible, relational, and still full of secrets.

title: military history companion|logistics failures on the Eastern Front in 1941
text:
The study of military history is often drawn to the drama of battle, to the clash of arms and the decisions of commanders at the decisive point. Yet behind every engagement lies a less glamorous, though no less critical, reality: the problem of supply. In the vast theater of the Eastern Front in 1941, this problem ceased to be a background concern and became a decisive factor in its own right, shaping and ultimately crippling the German advance. The story of Operation Barbarossa is, in large part, a story of logistics failures.

The German plan for the invasion of the Soviet Union was predicated on a rapid campaign, a lightning war that would collapse the Soviet state before the vast distances and harsh conditions could take their toll. This assumption was the original sin of the campaign. The Wehrmacht was a largely horse-drawn army, with the bulk of its supplies moved by rail and then by horse and cart to the front. The Soviet railway network was a different gauge from the European standard, meaning that captured track could not be used until it was laboriously converted. As the panzer groups raced east, they outran their supply lines with astonishing speed. The further they advanced, the longer and more fragile the logistical tether became.

The consequences were felt at every level. Fuel shortages were chronic, frequently halting the advance of the very armored spearheads that were supposed to deliver the knockout blow. Ammunition had to be rationed, and the arrival of winter clothing was delayed until it was almost too late. The supply services, the Nachschubtruppen, performed miracles of improvisation, but they were asked to solve an insoluble equation: to support an army of over three million men across a front thousands of kilometers wide, with a transport fleet that was never sufficient for the task. The mud of autumn and the snows of winter turned the few usable roads into impassable quagmires, swallowing vehicles and further isolating the forward units.

These failures were not merely technical. They had profound operational consequences. The diversion of resources to secure supply lines, the constant need to pause and wait for fuel and ammunition, and the inability to exploit opportunities all stemmed from the army's precarious logistical position. The failure to take Moscow in 1941 is often attributed to the decision to divert forces to the south, but it is equally true that the army approaching the Soviet capital was exhausted and at the end of its supply chain. The logistical apparatus had reached its breaking point.

In the end, the German army in 1941 was a victim of its own success and its own flawed assumptions. It had conquered vast territories and destroyed millions of Soviet troops, but it had done so at a rate that its supply system could not sustain. The Eastern Front was not a failure of fighting spirit or tactical skill, but of the mundane and unforgiving arithmetic of supply. The campaign of 1941 remains a stark lesson in the primacy of logistics, a reminder that in war, the question of how an army is fed, fueled, and armed is as decisive as any question of strategy or tactics.

title: journalism / narrative non-fiction|a town's struggle after its only factory closes
text:
The last whistle at Harland & Sons blew at 4:47 p.m. on a Friday in March, seven minutes ahead of schedule, which felt to everyone on the floor like the plant’s final small cruelty. Dale Varney, who had run the number-two stamping line for nineteen years, stood in the parking lot with his lunchbox still in his hand and watched the lights go off in the windows of the building his father had retired out of in 1994. “I kept waiting to feel something,” he told me later, at the kitchen table of the house on Cherry Street where he’s lived since he was twenty-six. “But it was like getting a flu shot. You know it’s coming, and then it’s done, and you just drive home.”

Harland made brake calipers, and for sixty-one years it made them in Millbrook, population 4,200, tucked into the folded hills of western Pennsylvania. At its peak the plant employed 1,100 people; on its last day, 214. The closure was announced the previous September in a two-paragraph press release that cited “consolidation of North American operations.” The company’s executives did not come to town. They sent a human resources consultant from Columbus who held four sessions in the high school cafeteria and handed out binders with tabs labeled *COBRA* and *Résumé Basics*.

The arithmetic of what happens next is not complicated. The plant’s payroll was roughly $14 million a year. The Millbrook Diner, which used to sell ninety breakfasts before six a.m., now sells thirty. The hardware store on Canal Street cut its hours in April and closed in July. The school district, which gets a third of its funding from property taxes, has already sent letters about next year’s bus routes. Pastor Jim Okonkwo at First Methodist told me his food pantry served forty families a month in 2019. Last month it served two hundred and six, and eleven of them drove in from the next county.

There is a particular kind of quiet that settles on a town in the months after the machines stop. You hear it on a Tuesday morning on Main Street: not silence exactly, but the absence of the sounds that used to fill it—the shift-change traffic, the idling diesels at the loading dock, the guys in the Harland hoodies standing outside the Sunoco at 6:15 with their coffee. The building itself still stands, fenced now, its windows papered over with that silver insulation wrap. Weeds have come up through the cracks in the employee lot. Someone—nobody will say who—painted a single word on the north wall in white block letters: *GONE*.

Dale Varney is fifty-eight. He has applied for thirty-one jobs since March. He has had two interviews, both in warehouses an hour away, both offering $16.50 an hour against the $24.80 he made at Harland. His wife, Renee, works part-time at the pharmacy. Their youngest is a sophomore at Millbrook High. When I asked him what he does with his days now, he looked out the window at the yard for a while and said, “I fix things that aren’t broke. Renee says I’m going to wear out the hinge on the screen door.” Then he laughed, and then he didn’t.
